newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada renew fight over farm trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada renew fight over farm trade.

text.p: The United States and Canada, the world's biggest trading partners, renewed their battle over agricultural trade on Tuesday, with Washington issuing a preemptive warning on imports of Canadian wheat.

The two countries have had an uneasy truce for the past year, largely because of market conditions. But U.S. wheat growers now fear there could be a return this year to surging imports of Canadian durum wheat experienced in 1994 and 1993.
The U.S. administration said it would monitor the trade situation closely in the next 12 months and seek consultations with Ottawa before imports reach disruptive levels.

"Following consultations, the administration will use appropriate U.S. trade laws if it appears likely that market disruption will occur," said Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman in a joint statement.

Ottawa reacted swiftly, promising retaliation for any unilateral trade action and saying that under the rules of the new World Trade Organisation the United States was no longer in a position to control trade flows.
"(There is) nothing that they can use on a unilateral basis that would not bring with it consequences flowing the other way," Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale told Reuters.

The two countries agreed in a Memorandum of Understanding in 1994 to cap Canadian wheat sales to the United States at 1.5 million metric tons for the year ending Sept. 11, 1995, to head off a trade war stemming from the surging imports.

The dispute has subsided in the year since the memorandum expired, because U.S. supplies were more abundant, because the United States has refrained from subsidising exports and there was no price differential favouring sales to the the United States.

But associations representing U.S. wheat growers and exporters said there are dangers of renewed import surges in the next 12 months, because of Canada's large wheat crop and the U.S. milling and baking industries' needs for wheat.
"They're already looking to undercut U.S. prices," said Nelson Denlinger, a spokesman for industry export promotion group U.S. Wheat Associates, which welcomed the U.S. government statement.
Canadian agriculture officials said that wheat exports to the United States in the next year would be less than the 1.5- million-ton cap agreed for 1994/95 under the Memorandum of Understanding.

"In fact, the volume trend over the last many months has been downwards, not upwards," Goodale said, adding that the move was difficult to understand except in terms of the upcoming U.S. presidential elections in November.
The U.S. administration has come under repeated pressure from lawmakers from Northern Plains states to confront the Canadian Wheat Board's sales practices.

Washington also complains that Canada has imposed excessively high tariffs on imports of U.S. dairy, egg and poultry products, but a preliminary ruling by a North American Free Trade Agreement panel earlier this year found in Canada's favour on that issue.
